content.title: About
content.content: Grits are a coarse ground corn product that originated in the United States. They have a mild, slightly sweet flavor and a creamy texture when cooked. Grits are commonly used as a side dish, breakfast base, or ingredient in Southern cuisine.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Grits became popular in the 19th‑century American South as an inexpensive source of energy for farmers.
Traditional preparation uses milk or broth, often finished with butter, cheese, or spices.
There are several varieties: quick‑cooking (fine) and regular (coarser) grits.
In Southern states grits are frequently served with bacon, eggs, or seafood.
Corn, the grain used for grits, is one of the oldest cultivated crops in the world.

items.title: Source of complex carbs
items.content: Grits provide sustained energy through slow‑release glucose.

items.title: Rich in fiber
items.content: Fiber supports digestive health and helps regulate blood sugar levels.

items.title: Contains vitamin B6
items.content: Vitamin B6 is involved in protein metabolism and neurotransmitter synthesis.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Grits contain very little saturated fat, making them suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: Provides magnesium and iron
items.content: These minerals are important for muscle function and oxygen transport.

items.title: Corn allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to corn products.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Grits can raise blood sugar quickly, so people with diabetes should monitor portion size.

items.title: Potential aflatoxin contamination
items.content: Poor‑quality corn may contain aflatoxins; choose reputable brands.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cook grits using a ratio of 1 part grits to 4–5 parts liquid (water, milk, or broth) for 15–20 minutes until tender. Serve with butter, cheese, herbs, vegetables, meat, or incorporate into casseroles and soups.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store grits in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. For long‑term storage keep them in the refrigerator or freezer to prevent mold growth.
